opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's changed quite a lot, actually. When we started, our view was fairly simple: release very strong open-weight models, make them efficient, and the community and enterprises would take them and run with them. That worked well for the developer community. People were fine-tuning, quantizing, building on top of the models almost immediately.

With enterprises, we realized pretty quickly that having a good model is necessary but far from sufficient. Many of these companies don't have large ML teams. Even the ones that do often struggle with the steps between "we downloaded the weights" and "this is running reliably in production on our data." So you get questions like: how do we deploy this on our own infrastructure, sometimes fully on-prem or air-gapped? How do we evaluate whether it's actually good for our use case? How do we fine-tune it on our internal data without leaking anything? How do we connect it to our documents, tools, and workflows?

So over time we've invested much more in the full stack around the models: deployment tooling, fine-tuning, and having our own applied engineers work directly with customers. Often the biggest gains don't come from a better base model. They come from understanding the customer's problem, building the right evaluation, getting the right data, and specializing a model for that task. A smaller model fine-tuned well can beat a much bigger general model and be far cheaper to serve.

The other thing we underestimated was how much sovereignty and control matter. Many customers, especially in Europe, in regulated industries, and in the public sector, really care about where their data goes and about not depending entirely on an API they don't control. Being able to give them the weights and help them run everything themselves turned out to be a big differentiator. It also means we need to support them much more closely than if we were just exposing an endpoint.

So I'd say we moved from thinking of ourselves mostly as a model provider to thinking of ourselves as a partner helping companies actually get value out of AI. The models are still the core, but the support around them matters a lot more than we initially thought.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, in the beginning we were quite naive about this. When we started Mistral, the mindset was very much a research mindset. We thought, if we train a great model and release the weights, people will figure out the rest. That's how it works in the research community. You put something on Hugging Face, people download it, they fine-tune it, they write the blog posts, they solve their own problems. And for the first wave of users, the developers and the hackers, that was true. Mistral 7B worked that way. We put a magnet link on Twitter and the community did an enormous amount for us.

But the moment we started talking to actual enterprises, we realized that the model is maybe twenty percent of what they need. The other eighty percent is everything around it. They want to know how to deploy it on their own infrastructure, which GPUs, what inference stack, how to do quantization without losing quality. They want to know how to fine-tune on their data, and often they don't actually have clean data, so first you have to help them build a dataset. They want evaluation. This one surprised me the most. Most companies have no idea how to measure whether a model is good for their use case. They have a feeling, they try a few prompts, but they don't have a benchmark that reflects their business. So a lot of what we do now is help them construct that.

And then there's the whole dimension of trust and governance, which, coming from research, I simply didn't think about. Where does the data go, who can see it, is it compliant, can we run it in an air-gapped environment. For many European customers, in banking or defense or healthcare, this is not a nice-to-have, it's the whole reason they are talking to us instead of using an API from somewhere else. So open weights turned out to matter for reasons that were partly different from what we expected. It wasn't only about the community. It was about control.

So I'd say our understanding went from "we ship models" to "we ship a way of working with models." That changed the company. We built a much bigger forward-deployed team than I would have guessed, people who sit with the customer for weeks. We built tooling for fine-tuning and evaluation that we originally only had internally. And it also feeds back into research, because when you see what breaks in deployment, you learn what to fix in the next model. The gap between a nice benchmark score and something that works in a customer's workflow is still larger than most people in the field admit.

r002.rationale: It describes added deployment needs such as infrastructure, fine-tuning, evaluation, and governance, but does not say that expanding model capabilities beyond text instruction following increased that complexity.

astra-6.text:
I think initially we underestimated how much work there is between having a good model and having something useful in production. As researchers, we tend to focus on the model itself: how capable it is, how it performs on benchmarks. But for a customer, that’s only one part of the problem. They need to connect it to their data, evaluate it on their use case, and deploy it within their infrastructure and constraints.

So our understanding has shifted from providing models to helping people build applications around them. Sometimes the answer is a better model, but sometimes it’s changing how you retrieve information or how you evaluate the output. And that requires working closely with the customer. You learn a lot more about what matters when you see where a deployment actually gets stuck.

sol-6.1.text:
At the beginning, we thought that if we released a good model, people would be able to take it and build what they needed. And some customers can do that, but for many, the model is only one part of the problem. They need help figuring out how to deploy it in their environment, connect it to their data, and evaluate whether it’s actually doing the job well.

So our understanding has become much more end to end. It’s not just, “Here are the weights.” It’s understanding the use case and helping the customer get to something that works in production. And the level of support varies a lot depending on the team and what they’re trying to build.
